elaboracion.title: How Wine Is Made
elaboracion.intro: You'll follow the path from grape to glass: what happens during fermentation, why a wine ends up red, white or rosé, and what oak, time and the bottle add.

chapters.lead: Wine is fermented grape juice: yeasts eat the grape's sugar and turn it into alcohol and carbon dioxide.
points: It all starts with the harvest: picking the grapes when the winery decides they are ripe.
At the winery, grapes are destemmed (the stems, the woody part of the bunch, are removed) and crushed to break the skins and release the juice, now called must.
Alcoholic fermentation: yeasts turn sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide (CO2), and also give off heat.
The most common yeast is Saccharomyces cerevisiae; it can come from the grapes and the winery (native or ambient yeast) or be added as a selected strain.
If yeasts eat almost all the sugar, the wine is dry; many yeasts can't survive above about 15% alcohol.
Careful: the juice of almost all grapes is colourless. Wine gets its colour from the skins, and that decides whether it is red, white or rosé.

keys.t: Picking the grapes to make wine.
Separating the grapes from the stems, the woody frame of the bunch.
Grape juice (with or without skins) before it becomes wine.
A microscopic fungus that turns sugar into alcohol and CO2.
The process in which yeasts convert the sugar in the must into alcohol and carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: What do yeasts produce when they eat the sugar in the must?
quiz.ok: Alcohol and carbon dioxide (CO2)
quiz.why: Alcoholic fermentation turns sugar into alcohol and CO2, and releases heat.

quiz.q: Where does the colour of a red wine come from?
quiz.ok: From the grape skin
bad: From the juice, which is already red
quiz.why: The juice of almost all grapes is colourless: the colour is extracted from the skins.

quiz.q: What is destemming?
quiz.ok: Separating the grapes from the stems of the bunch
quiz.why: Destemming means removing the stems before crushing the grapes.

chapters.t: Red wine: fermenting with the skins
chapters.lead: Red wine ferments together with the skins. That contact gives it colour, tannins and aromas; only afterwards is it pressed.
points: The must ferments with skins and seeds: this maceration extracts colour, tannins and flavour.
The skins rise and form a "cap"; it is pushed down (punching down) or sprayed with must from below (pumping over) to keep extracting.
It ferments warmer than a white wine: roughly between 20 and 32 °C. More heat and more time mean more extraction.
As time goes on, less colour and more tannin are extracted; wines meant for ageing can stay extra weeks on the skins.
At the end the wine is pressed: it is separated from the skins.
The variety matters: thin-skinned Pinot Noir gives less colour than thick-skinned Cabernet Sauvignon.

keys.t: The skin of the grape, which holds the colour and a good part of the tannins and aromas.
Leaving the must or wine in contact with the skins to extract colour, tannins and flavour.
Compounds from skins and seeds that give that rough, drying feeling in the mouth.
The layer of skins that floats on top of the tank during red wine fermentation.
Squeezing the grapes or skins to separate the liquid from the solids.

quiz.q: In a red wine, when is the pressing done?
quiz.ok: After fermenting with the skins
bad: Before fermenting, like a white wine
Right before bottling, after the barrel
quiz.why: Red wine ferments with the skins to take on colour and tannins, and only then is it separated with the press.

quiz.q: What happens if contact with the skins is made longer?
quiz.ok: The wine gains more colour and tannins
bad: The wine loses all its alcohol
quiz.why: More maceration time and temperature mean more extraction.

quiz.q: What are pumping over and punching down for?
quiz.ok: To keep the must in contact with the cap of skins
quiz.why: The skins float, and wetting or pushing them down allows colour and tannins to keep being extracted.

chapters.lead: For white wine the skins are removed before fermentation; for rosé they stay just a short while, enough to tint the juice.
points: White: the grapes are pressed before fermentation and only the juice ferments, without skins; that is why it has almost no tannins.
It ferments cooler than red, roughly between 12 and 22 °C, almost always in stainless steel tanks.
White wine can be made from red grapes if the juice is separated right away, as in Champagne; still, almost all whites come from white grapes.
Rosé by short maceration: red grapes stay on their skins from a few hours up to about two days; then the juice is separated and ferments like a white.
Direct pressing: red grapes are pressed right away, giving the palest rosés.
Saignée (bleeding): some juice is drawn off a red wine tank early in the maceration, and that juice is fermented as rosé.

keys.t: Pressing the grapes as soon as they arrive, without letting the juice sit on the skins.
Brief contact of the juice with red grape skins to give it a pink colour.
Drawing off part of the juice from a red wine tank at the start to make rosé.
A tank material that adds no flavour and allows good temperature control.

quiz.q: How does making white wine differ from making red?
quiz.ok: White is pressed before fermentation, without skins
bad: White ferments on the skins for weeks
quiz.why: White ferments only the juice, and at a lower temperature than red.

quiz.q: How is a rosé made by saignée?
quiz.ok: By drawing juice off a red wine tank at the start of maceration
bad: By leaving red grapes on the skins for weeks
By fermenting white grapes at high heat
By adding colouring to a white wine
quiz.why: Saignée means drawing off part of the pink juice early and fermenting it separately.

quiz.q: Can white wine be made from red grapes?
quiz.ok: Yes, if the juice is separated from the skins right away
bad: Yes, but only by adding water
Yes, only if it ferments in barrel
quiz.why: The juice is colourless: without skin contact the wine comes out white, as in Champagne.

chapters.lead: After alcoholic fermentation the wine can still change: bacteria soften the acidity and dead yeasts give creaminess.
points: Malolactic conversion is carried out by lactic bacteria (mainly Oenococcus oeni): they turn malic acid into softer lactic acid.
Result: less acidity and, sometimes, a buttery aroma from a compound called diacetyl.
It is a key step in almost all reds and in some whites, such as many Chardonnays.
Lees are the sediment left after fermentation, mostly dead yeast.
Ageing on the lees gives a creamier texture and aromas like brioche or nuts; it is typical of Muscadet, Champagne and white Burgundy.
Bâtonnage is stirring the lees so the wine has more contact with them.

keys.t: Bacteria turning malic acid into lactic acid; it lowers acidity.
A compound that can form during malolactic conversion and smells of butter.
Sediment of dead yeast and other particles left after fermentation.
A French expression for a wine aged in contact with its lees.
Stirring the lees inside the barrel or tank.

quiz.q: What is the main effect of malolactic conversion?
quiz.ok: It lowers the wine's acidity
quiz.why: The bacteria turn malic acid into lactic acid, which is softer.

quiz.q: What are lees?
quiz.ok: Sediment made mostly of dead yeast
quiz.why: Lees are the remains that settle after fermentation, mostly yeast.

quiz.q: A white wine with a buttery aroma probably went through…
quiz.ok: Malolactic conversion
quiz.why: The diacetyl that can form during malolactic conversion smells of butter.

chapters.lead: Where the wine rests changes how it tastes: steel adds nothing, while oak adds aromas, tannins and a little oxygen.
points: Wine can ferment or rest in stainless steel, concrete or oak.
Stainless steel is neutral: it adds no flavour, so the fruit aromas shine.
Oak adds aromas like vanilla, coconut, clove, caramel or smoke, and also tannins.
Wood lets in a little oxygen, which helps fix the colour and soften the wine.
A new barrel gives much more; after about four vintages it gives almost no oak flavour, but it still lets in oxygen.
Size: the Bordeaux barrique holds 225 litres; the smaller the barrel, the more contact with the wood and the more influence.

keys.t: An oak cask; the classic Bordeaux barrique holds 225 litres.
American oak usually gives stronger vanilla and coconut; French oak, subtler notes and firmer tannins.
The charring of the inside of the barrel when it is made; it shapes the aromas it gives.
A barrel that has held several vintages; it gives little flavour but still lets in oxygen.

quiz.q: What does stainless steel add to the flavour of wine?
quiz.ok: Nothing: it is a neutral material
quiz.why: Steel gives off no flavours; vanilla or toasty aromas come from oak.

quiz.q: Which barrel marks the wine most with oak flavour?
quiz.ok: A small, new barrel
bad: A barrel from ten vintages ago
quiz.why: New wood gives more, and in small barrels each litre touches more wood.

quiz.q: Besides aromas, what does oak do?
quiz.ok: It lets in some oxygen and adds tannins
bad: It adds sugar to the wine
It carries out malolactic conversion by itself
quiz.why: Wood is porous: it oxygenates slowly and gives off tannins.

chapters.lead: Before bottling, the wine is cleaned and stabilised so it reaches your glass in good shape; some wines also improve with years in bottle.
points: Fining: products like egg white or bentonite (a clay) are added to carry away particles and soften harsh tannins.
Filtration: physically removes particles and microbes before bottling.
Stabilisation: cold or bentonite treatments so no crystals or haze appear in the bottle.
Sulphur dioxide (sulphites) protects the wine from oxygen and slows bacteria.
Most wines are made to be drunk young; only some, with good acidity, tannins and intensity, improve with ageing.
In bottle, fruity aromas fade and others appear (nut, caramel, honey), and the tannins soften.

keys.t: Adding a product that traps suspended particles and makes them settle.
Passing the wine through a filter to remove particles and microbes.
A preservative that protects wine from oxidation and bacteria.
Those that appear with ageing and time, such as nut, caramel or honey.
The set of aromas wine gains from ageing in barrel and bottle.

quiz.q: What are sulphites used for in wine?
quiz.ok: To protect it from oxygen and bacteria
bad: To give it a red colour
quiz.why: Sulphur dioxide acts as an antioxidant and antimicrobial.

quiz.q: Do all wines get better if you keep them for years?
quiz.ok: No, most are made to be drunk young
bad: Yes, as long as they have a cork
quiz.why: Only a few, with good acidity, tannins and intensity, gain from ageing.

quiz.q: What happens to a red wine after years in bottle?
quiz.ok: Its tannins soften and tertiary aromas appear
bad: It becomes more acidic and fruity
quiz.why: Over time the tannins polish and fresh fruit gives way to notes like nut or caramel.

chapters.t: Reading ageing on the label: the example of Spain
chapters.lead: Some countries regulate words on the label that tell you how long the wine was aged. Spain is the best-known example.
points: In Spain, Law 24/2003 on Vine and Wine defines Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva for wines with a designation of origin.
Red Crianza: minimum 24 months of ageing, at least 6 of them in oak barrel.
Red Reserva: minimum 36 months, at least 12 in oak; the rest in bottle.
Red Gran Reserva: minimum 60 months, at least 18 in oak.
"Joven" (young) is used for wines of the year, with little or no oak ageing.
Each designation can demand more (Rioja requires 12 months in barrel for a red Crianza). They show ageing time, not quality.

keys.t: Wine of the year, meant to be drunk fresh, with little or no ageing.
In Spain, a red with at least 2 years of ageing, 6 months in oak.
In Spain, a red with at least 3 years of ageing, 1 year in oak.
In Spain, a red with at least 5 years of ageing, 18 months in oak.

quiz.q: Under Spanish law, what is the minimum ageing of a red Reserva?
quiz.ok: 36 months, with at least 12 in oak
quiz.why: Law 24/2003 sets 36 months of ageing, 12 of them in wood, for a red Reserva.

quiz.q: Which term means the longest ageing in a Spanish red?
quiz.ok: Gran Reserva
quiz.why: Gran Reserva requires at least 60 months, more than Reserva (36) and Crianza (24).

quiz.q: What does the word "Reserva" tell you on a Spanish label?
quiz.ok: The minimum time the wine was aged
bad: That it comes from a single vineyard
quiz.why: These terms regulate ageing time, not quality or other attributes.

vinedo.title: Vineyard, Climate and Labels
vinedo.intro: You'll understand where what you drink comes from: the grape, the vineyard's year, the climate and the soil. And you'll be able to read a label without getting lost.

chapters.lead: Each part of the bunch adds something different to the wine. Knowing them explains why a red has colour and tannins, and a white doesn't.
points: The pulp is most of the grape: water, sugar, acids and aroma precursors. The juice comes from there.
The skin adds colour, aromas typical of each variety and tannins. The colour of red wine comes from here.
The seeds give harder, more bitter tannins; that's why they should be ripe and not be crushed.
The stem (the bunch's 'skeleton') holds the grapes; it is almost always removed because it can give green, astringent notes.
Wine grapes have thicker skins, more seeds and more sugar than table grapes.

keys.t: The skin of the grape; it holds the colour, a good part of the aroma and tannins.
The flesh of the grape, with the water, sugar and acids that make up the juice.
The branching stalk that holds the grapes in the bunch.
Substances from skin, seeds and stems that give that rough feeling that dries the mouth.
Separating the grapes from the stems before winemaking.

quiz.q: Where does the colour of a red wine come from?
quiz.ok: From the skin
quiz.why: The red pigments are in the skin, and the wine takes them up by staying in contact with it.

quiz.q: Which part of the grape provides most of the juice?
quiz.ok: The pulp
quiz.why: The pulp is most of the grape and holds the water, sugar and acids.

quiz.q: Why is the stem almost always removed?
quiz.ok: Because it can give green, astringent notes
bad: Because it holds all the sugar
Because it gives the wine its colour
quiz.why: The stem holds up the bunch, but it doesn't add what is wanted and can give green, harsh flavours.

chapters.lead: The vine repeats the same cycle every year: it wakes up, flowers, ripens the grapes and rests. In the southern hemisphere everything happens about six months out of step with the north.
points: Budburst: the vine wakes up and shoots appear. In the south, around September; in the north, around March.
Flowering and fruit set: the flower becomes a tiny berry. In the south, around November; in the north, around May.
Véraison: the grape changes colour, softens, gathers sugar and loses acidity. In the south, late January to February.
Harvest: in the south, February to April; in the north, September to October.
Dormancy and pruning: after the leaves fall, the vine rests and is pruned in winter. Uruguay follows the southern hemisphere calendar.

keys.t: When the vine wakes up in spring and the first shoots appear.
When the vine flowers; each fertilised flower becomes a berry.
The moment when the grape changes colour and starts to ripen.
Picking the grapes.
The winter cutting of the plant to organise how much and where it will produce.

quiz.q: What happens at véraison?
quiz.ok: The grape changes colour and starts to ripen
quiz.why: At véraison the grape colours, softens, gathers sugar and its acidity drops.

quiz.q: In Uruguay (southern hemisphere), when is the harvest generally?
quiz.ok: Between February and April
bad: In the middle of winter, in July
quiz.why: In the southern hemisphere the harvest falls in late summer and autumn, from February to April.

quiz.q: At what time of year is the vine pruned?
quiz.ok: In winter, when the plant is dormant
quiz.why: Pruning is done during winter dormancy, before the vine buds again.

chapters.lead: Climate is one of the things that changes wine most. In the cold the grape keeps acidity; in the warmth it gathers more sugar, and that sugar becomes alcohol.
points: Cool climate: wines with higher acidity, lower alcohol, lighter body and less tannin.
Warm climate: more alcohol, more body and more tannin, with less acidity and riper fruit; with too much sun, jammy notes.
Latitude: the closer to the equator, the warmer. Almost all vineyards lie between 30° and 50° latitude.
Altitude: the higher the vineyard, the cooler.
Sea and continentality: the sea moderates temperatures. Far from the sea, the gap between summer and winter is bigger (continental climate).
Uruguay: in the south, where most Tannat is planted (the most planted grape, INAVI 2023), the climate is temperate-warm with a sea breeze.

keys.t: The freshness of the wine, what makes you salivate; it is better preserved in cool climates.
The feeling of weight of the wine in the mouth.
Climate near the sea, with little temperature difference between summer and winter.
The difference in temperature between the hottest and coldest month of a place.
A cool wind from the sea that tempers the heat in vineyards near the coast.

quiz.q: In general, a wine from a cool climate has…
quiz.ok: More acidity and less alcohol
quiz.why: In the cold the grape keeps its acidity and gathers less sugar, which is what turns into alcohol.

quiz.q: In Uruguayan vineyards closest to the Río de la Plata, the temperature difference between day and night is…
quiz.ok: Smaller
quiz.why: Water moderates temperature, so near the coast day and night are more alike.

quiz.q: What does the sea do to the climate of a nearby vineyard?
quiz.ok: It moderates temperatures
bad: It increases the gap between summer and winter
quiz.why: Large bodies of water soften extremes; that is why a maritime climate varies little through the year.

chapters.lead: Soil matters mostly because of water: how much it holds and how fast it lets it go. Terroir is the sum of the place and of what people do in it.
points: The most important thing about soil is water: a gravelly soil drains fast; a clay soil holds more.
Too much water can give swollen, rotten grapes; a little water stress is associated with smaller, more concentrated grapes.
Stones and dark soils store heat and give it back at night; this helps mostly in cool climates.
Myth: wine doesn't 'taste' of the rocks in the soil. The plant only takes up nutrients dissolved in water.
Terroir (OIV): an area where the physical environment and the grape grower's practices, known together, give wines with their own traits.

keys.t: The combination of soil, climate, relief and local know-how that gives identity to the wines of a place.
How fast rainwater passes through the soil and drains away.
When the vine has less water than it would like; in the right dose, it concentrates the grape.
A soil of small stones that drains very well.
A soil of very fine particles that holds a lot of water.

quiz.q: What is the most direct contribution of soil to wine?
quiz.ok: How much water the vine receives
bad: Passing the flavour of its rocks to the wine
quiz.why: Specialists agree that soil acts mainly through water; the flavour of rocks doesn't pass into the wine.

quiz.q: A gravelly soil, in general…
quiz.ok: Drains very fast
bad: Holds lots of water, like clay
quiz.why: The stones let water through easily.

quiz.q: According to the OIV, terroir includes…
quiz.ok: The natural environment and the practices of those who work the vineyard
bad: Only the type of rock in the soil
quiz.why: The OIV definition joins soil, climate, relief and biodiversity with the grape grower's know-how.

chapters.lead: A vine left alone spends energy growing and climbing. The grape grower guides it so that energy goes into ripening good grapes.
points: The vine is a climber: it needs support. In the vineyard, training systems are used, such as the vertical trellis.
The trellis arranges the plant vertically to manage the leaves and how much sun the bunches get.
Yield: a very vigorous vine gives many grapes of medium quality; a less vigorous one gives fewer grapes, but more concentrated.
Irrigation: where summers are dry, drip irrigation lets you control how much water the plant receives.
Organic: no synthetic pesticides or chemical fertilisers. Biodynamic: adds special preparations and astronomical rhythms; it is often Demeter certified.

keys.t: The way the plant is guided and supported in the vineyard.
A system of wires where the vine grows vertically, like a green wall.
How much fruit is harvested per plant or per hectare.
How much a vine grows and produces.
Organic farming with its own preparations and calendar; it grew out of the ideas of Rudolf Steiner.

quiz.q: In general, what happens if a vine bears a huge number of grapes?
quiz.ok: The grapes tend to be less concentrated
bad: The wine automatically comes out redder
quiz.why: The plant's energy is spread over more bunches, so each grape concentrates less.

quiz.q: What is a trellis for?
quiz.ok: To organise the plant and manage the sun on the bunches
bad: To protect the grapes from birds in the winery
quiz.why: It is a training system that guides the vine vertically.

quiz.q: What characterises an organic vineyard?
quiz.ok: It uses no synthetic pesticides or chemical fertilisers
bad: It irrigates every day without limit
quiz.why: Organic farming avoids synthetic chemicals and uses natural fertilisers.

chapters.lead: Old World is Europe, the cradle of modern wine traditions; New World is the countries that adopted them later, like Uruguay. Today the terms are used more for styles than for maps.
points: Old World: France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, Germany and other European countries. New World: the Americas, South Africa, Australia, New Zealand, China.
Typical Old World style: lighter body and alcohol, more acidity, less fruit. It is often tied to cooler climates.
Typical New World style: fuller body and alcohol, less acidity and pronounced fruit. It is a tendency, not a rule.
The Old World has stricter rules and usually names the wine by region; the New World, by grape.
There are exceptions: Italy has warm areas with fruit-rich wines, and Alsace (France) puts the grape on the label.

keys.t: The European countries where modern wine traditions were born.
The countries that adopted those traditions later, often through colonisation.
A wine presented under the name of its grape.
The general profile of a wine: body, acidity, alcohol, fruit.

quiz.q: Is Uruguay Old World or New World?
quiz.ok: New World
quiz.why: Everything outside Europe that adopted the European tradition is considered New World.

quiz.q: How is an Old World wine usually named on the label?
quiz.ok: By its region of origin
quiz.why: Its laws are based mostly on place, so the region is the main piece of information.

quiz.q: The 'typical' New World style is…
quiz.ok: Fuller body and fruit, less acidity
quiz.why: It is usually associated with warmer climates, though there are many exceptions.

chapters.lead: A label has mandatory information and other details the producer chooses to include. Once you know which is which, you can place almost any wine.
points: Mandatory in the European Union: origin, category or appellation, alcoholic strength, volume, bottler, allergens (sulphites) and lot.
Grape and vintage are optional. If shown, the wine must contain at least 85% of that grape and 85% from that year.
DO (Denominación de Origen): a protected area with its own rules; the place name guarantees the origin.
Spain example (Law 24/2003): red Crianza, minimum 24 months (6 in oak); Reserva, 36 (12 in oak); Gran Reserva, 60 (18 in oak).
In Uruguay you will see 'VCP' (Vino de Calidad Preferente): wine made from vinifera grapes of recognised quality, under national regulations.

keys.t: The year the grapes were harvested, not the year of bottling.
Denominación de Origen: the name of a protected area, with rules on grapes and winemaking.
In Spain, a red with at least 36 months of ageing, 12 of them in oak barrel.
Vino de Calidad Preferente, a Uruguayan category for wines from quality vinifera grapes.
The percentage of alcohol in the wine, in % vol.

quiz.q: In the European Union, if the label says 'Tempranillo', the wine must contain at least…
quiz.ok: 85% Tempranillo
quiz.why: European rules require a minimum of 85% of the named grape.

quiz.q: What does the vintage indicate?
quiz.ok: The year the grapes were harvested
bad: How many years the winery has existed
quiz.why: The vintage is the year of the harvest.

quiz.q: In Spain, which red has the longest minimum ageing?
quiz.ok: Gran Reserva
quiz.why: Gran Reserva requires 60 months, against 36 for Reserva and 24 for Crianza.

estilos.title: Wine Styles
estilos.intro: By the end you'll be able to place any wine on the map: still or sparkling, dry or sweet, light or powerful, and understand how sparkling wines, sweet wines, Port and Sherry are made.

chapters.lead: Almost every wine fits into a few families: still white, rosé and red, sparkling, sweet and fortified. Within each, wines are ordered by body (light to full) and by sweetness (dry to sweet).
points: Still means a wine without bubbles: the everyday kind, white, rosé or red.
Light reds: Pinot Noir or Gamay. Medium: Merlot or Sangiovese. Full-bodied: Cabernet Sauvignon, Syrah, Malbec or Tannat.
Light, dry whites: Sauvignon Blanc or Albariño. Fuller: oaked Chardonnay or Viognier. Aromatic: Riesling, Torrontés, Muscat.
Rosé comes from red grapes whose skins touch the juice for a short time, usually between 2 and 24 hours.
More body usually goes hand in hand with more alcohol and, in reds, more tannin.
Sweetness doesn't come from the grape: the winemaker decides it. A Riesling can be dry or sweet.

keys.t: Wine without bubbles, whether white, rosé or red.
The feeling of weight of the wine in the mouth, from light to full.
Grape sugar left unconverted into alcohol; it is what makes a wine sweet.
The time the juice stays in contact with the skins, from which it takes colour and tannins.

quiz.q: Where does the colour of a rosé come from?
quiz.ok: From short contact of the juice with red grape skins
bad: From adding colouring to white wine
From a special pink grape used only for rosé
From ageing it for years in barrel
quiz.why: The juice of almost all grapes is clear; colour comes from red skins, and in rosé that contact lasts only a few hours.

quiz.q: Which of these would be a light red?
quiz.ok: Pinot Noir
quiz.why: Pinot Noir is the classic example of a light red; the others are full-bodied reds.

quiz.q: What makes a wine sweet?
quiz.ok: Grape sugar that was not converted into alcohol
bad: The grape simply being a 'sweet' variety
quiz.why: Sweetness is residual sugar and depends on winemaking, not on the variety.

chapters.lead: In the traditional method the bubbles are born inside the very bottle you'll open, thanks to a second fermentation. This is how Champagne and Cava are made.
points: It starts from a dry base wine, bottled with a mix of sugar and yeast (liqueur de tirage).
In the sealed bottle the second fermentation takes place: the gas can't escape and stays dissolved. In Champagne it reaches about 6 bar.
The wine rests on its lees, the dead yeast, which give notes of bread and dough. Champagne requires at least 15 months, and 36 for vintage.
Riddling: the bottles are gradually turned and tilted to gather the lees in the neck.
Disgorgement: that deposit is expelled and the bottle is topped up with the dosage (liqueur d'expédition), which sets the final sweetness.
Cava uses the same method, with at least 9 months of ageing in bottle; the higher categories require considerably more.

keys.t: A new fermentation of the finished wine, which creates the gas for the bubbles.
The dead yeast left in the bottle that adds toasty bread and dough aromas.
Gradually turning and tilting the bottles to bring the lees to the neck.
Removing the plug of lees collected in the neck of the bottle.
The wine, with or without sugar, added after disgorgement; it sets whether it is Brut, Demi-sec, etc.

quiz.q: In the traditional method, where does the second fermentation take place?
quiz.ok: In the same bottle that reaches your table
bad: There is no second fermentation: gas is injected
quiz.why: What defines the traditional method is that the bubbles form in the bottle itself.

quiz.q: What is disgorgement for?
quiz.ok: To remove the lees collected in the neck of the bottle
bad: To add the original yeast again
To chill the wine before selling it
To blend white and red grapes
quiz.why: After riddling, the lees sit in the neck and disgorgement expels them.

quiz.q: What do Champagne and Cava have in common?
quiz.ok: Both are made by the traditional method
bad: Both are made in a closed tank
quiz.why: Champagne and Cava carry out their second fermentation in bottle and age on the lees.

chapters.lead: Not all bubbles are made in bottle. Prosecco does its second fermentation in large closed tanks, and the ancestral method uses a single fermentation that finishes in the bottle.
points: Tank method (Charmat or Martinotti): the second fermentation takes place in large pressurised sealed tanks, called autoclaves.
Afterwards the wine is filtered and bottled with its bubbles already in.
It is the method of Prosecco, made mostly from the Glera grape; it aims for freshness and fruit, to be drunk young.
Ancestral (and its modern version, pét-nat): the wine is bottled before it finishes fermenting and fermentation carries on in the bottle.
Ancestral has less pressure (about 3 to 3.5 bar against 6 for Champagne) and is sometimes a little cloudy, with its yeast still in.

keys.t: A method in which the second fermentation takes place in a closed pressurised tank.
A large sealed tank that withstands pressure, where Prosecco's bubbles are formed.
The main grape of Prosecco.
A single-fermentation sparkling wine that starts in tank and finishes inside the bottle.
Pétillant naturel: the modern name for sparkling wines made by the ancestral method.

quiz.q: Where does Prosecco do its second fermentation?
quiz.ok: In large closed tanks (autoclaves)
bad: It doesn't ferment: carbon dioxide is added
quiz.why: Prosecco uses the Martinotti or Charmat method, in a pressurised tank.

quiz.q: What distinguishes the ancestral method?
quiz.ok: It has a single fermentation that finishes in the bottle
bad: It is always made in an autoclave
It must rest 36 months on the lees
quiz.why: In the ancestral method the wine is bottled before it finishes fermenting.

quiz.q: Compared with Champagne, an ancestral wine usually has…
quiz.ok: Less pressure and a softer mousse
quiz.why: Ancestral sits around 3 to 3.5 bar, against about 6 bar for the traditional method.

chapters.t: Brut, Extra Brut and the rest
chapters.lead: The label of a sparkling wine tells you how much sugar it has. In the European Union each word has an official range in grams per litre.
points: Brut Nature: less than 3 g/L. Extra Brut: 0 to 6 g/L. Brut: less than 12 g/L.
Extra Dry: 12 to 17 g/L. Sec (Dry): 17 to 32 g/L.
Demi-sec (Medium Dry): 32 to 50 g/L. Doux (Sweet): more than 50 g/L.
Watch out for the trap: 'Extra Dry' is sweeter than 'Brut', even though it sounds drier.
The final sweetness is mostly set by the dosage added after disgorgement.

keys.t: Grams of sugar per litre of wine.
The driest: less than 3 g/L of sugar.
The most common style: less than 12 g/L of sugar.
Medium dry: between 32 and 50 g/L, clearly tastes sweet.
The amount of sugar contributed by the liqueur d'expédition.

quiz.q: Which of these sparkling wines is the driest?
quiz.ok: Brut Nature
quiz.why: Brut Nature has less than 3 g/L, the bottom of the scale.

quiz.q: Between a Brut and an Extra Dry, which is sweeter?
quiz.ok: The Extra Dry
bad: It depends only on the grape
quiz.why: Brut is less than 12 g/L and Extra Dry runs from 12 to 17 g/L.

quiz.q: A sparkling wine with 40 g/L of sugar is labelled as…
quiz.ok: Demi-sec
quiz.why: Demi-sec covers 32 to 50 g/L.

chapters.lead: For a wine to be sweet without adding anything, you have to concentrate the grape's sugar or stop the fermentation. There are several routes: leaving the grape on the vine, a fungus, frost, or drying.
points: Late harvest: the grapes stay longer on the vine and concentrate sugar. In Alsace it is called Vendange Tardive; in Germany, Spätlese.
Noble rot: the fungus Botrytis cinerea pierces the grape skin, and the grape dehydrates and concentrates. This is how Sauternes (Sémillon) and Tokaji Aszú (Furmint) are born.
It needs humid mornings with river mist and dry afternoons; it brings notes of honey, ginger and saffron.
Ice wine: the grapes freeze naturally on the vine and are pressed frozen. In Canada they require -8 °C or lower.
Dried grapes: dried after harvest (appassimento). Recioto della Valpolicella stays sweet; Amarone, from the same grapes, ferments almost dry.

keys.t: Wine made from grapes left to ripen longer on the vine.
A fungus that, in the right climate, dehydrates the grape and concentrates its sugar: 'noble rot'.
Wine from grapes frozen on the vine and pressed that way, to extract only a very concentrated juice.
Drying harvested grapes to concentrate sugar and flavour.
Traditional measure of sweetness for Tokaji Aszú, named after the baskets used to gather botrytised grapes.

quiz.q: What does noble rot do to the grape?
quiz.ok: It pierces the skin, dehydrates it and concentrates the sugar
bad: It rots it and always makes it undrinkable
It freezes it on the vine
quiz.why: Botrytis opens microscopic pores in the skin, the grape loses water and the sugar concentrates.

quiz.q: How is a genuine ice wine made?
quiz.ok: With grapes naturally frozen on the vine and pressed frozen
bad: By adding ice to the finished wine
By keeping the wine in a freezer
quiz.why: The water stays as ice in the grape and only the concentrated juice is pressed out.

quiz.q: Amarone and Recioto are made from dried grapes. Which one stays sweet?
quiz.ok: Recioto
quiz.why: Recioto keeps residual sugar; Amarone ferments almost to dryness.

chapters.lead: Port is a wine from the Douro Valley in Portugal to which grape spirit is added while it ferments. That stops the yeast and leaves a sweet wine with more alcohol.
points: Grape spirit is added in the middle of fermentation, generally one part to every four of fermenting must. The yeast stops and sugar is left unfermented.
Result: a sweet wine of 19% to 22% alcohol.
Ruby style: aims to keep the deep red colour and fruit of a young wine. Includes Ruby, Reserve, LBV and Vintage.
Tawny style: blends of wines aged in wood; the colour turns amber and nutty and woody notes appear. There are 10, 20, 30 and 40 Year Old Tawnies.
LBV: a single-year Ruby, bottled after 4 to 6 years in wood; almost always ready to drink.
Vintage: from a single year, bottled at 2 or 3 years old and made to evolve for decades in bottle.

keys.t: A wine to which alcohol of grape origin is added.
Wine distillate used to fortify.
A red Port with young fruit and little oxidative development.
Port aged in wood, amber in colour with nutty notes.
Late Bottled Vintage: a single-year Ruby, bottled after 4 to 6 years in wood.

quiz.q: When is Port fortified?
quiz.ok: During fermentation, to stop it
bad: After the wine has finished fermenting dry
Never: it is sweet because of the grape
quiz.why: The spirit cuts the fermentation short, which is why unfermented sugar remains.

quiz.q: An amber Port with notes of walnut and wood is probably…
quiz.ok: A Tawny
quiz.why: Ageing in wood turns Tawny amber and gives it nutty notes.

quiz.q: Which is the only Port style made to age for decades in bottle?
quiz.ok: Vintage
quiz.why: Vintage is bottled at 2 or 3 years old and keeps evolving in bottle.

chapters.lead: Sherry, from southern Spain, is fortified after fermentation, when the wine is already dry. Depending on how much alcohol is added, it ages under a veil of yeast (flor) or in contact with air.
points: Grapes: Palomino for the dry styles; Pedro Ximénez and Moscatel for the sweet ones.
Fortified to 15%: flor grows, a veil of yeast that protects the wine from air. This is biological ageing: Fino and Manzanilla (from Sanlúcar de Barrameda).
Fortified to 17%: flor can't survive and the wine ages oxidatively, in contact with air. This is how Oloroso is born.
Amontillado: starts under flor like a Fino and then keeps ageing oxidatively. It has both kinds of ageing.
Solera and criaderas: barrels in tiers. A portion is drawn from the solera (the oldest) and topped up from the criadera above; this is the saca and rocío.
Pedro Ximénez: sun-dried grapes, fermentation stopped with alcohol; it never falls below 250 g/L of sugar.

keys.t: A veil of yeast over the wine that shields it from air and gives pungent, almond notes.
Ageing under flor, without contact with air: Fino and Manzanilla.
Ageing without flor, in contact with air: Oloroso.
The tier of barrels holding the oldest wine, from which bottling is drawn.
The tiers of barrels with younger wine that replenish the solera.

quiz.q: What is the difference between Fino and Oloroso?
quiz.ok: Fino ages under flor; Oloroso in contact with air
bad: Fino is sweet and Oloroso dry
Fino is from Portugal and Oloroso from Spain
Oloroso is made in a closed tank
quiz.why: Fino is biological ageing and Oloroso is oxidative ageing.

quiz.q: Why doesn't Oloroso develop flor?
quiz.ok: Because it is fortified to 17% and flor can't survive
bad: Because it is bottled right away
Because it is made from red grapes
Because it is kept in glass bottles
quiz.why: At 15% flor lives; at 17% it doesn't, and the wine slowly oxidises.

quiz.q: In the solera system, where does the bottled wine come from?
quiz.ok: From the solera, the tier with the oldest wine
bad: From a single new barrel each year
quiz.why: It is drawn from the solera and topped up from the criadera above, which is topped up from the next one.

estilos.sources: Wine Folly, The 9 Major Wine Styles (winefolly.com/tips/the-9-major-wine-styles); Wine Folly, What Is Rosé (winefolly.com/deep-dive/what-is-rose-wine); Wine Folly, Types of Dessert Wine (winefolly.com/deep-dive/types-dessert-wine); Reglamento Delegado (UE) 2019/33, Anexo III Parte A (legislation.gov.uk/eur/2019/33/annex/III); Comité Champagne, Fiche Élaboration Champagne (champagne.education); DO Cava, Nueva normativa (cava.wine/documents/225); Consorzio Prosecco DOC (prosecco.wine/en/prosecco); BKWine, Pétillant naturel en Montlouis (bkwine.com); Decanter, Sauternes vs Tokaji Aszú y Amarone vs Recioto (decanter.com/learn); Wine with Seth, Icewine (reglas VQA Canadá); IVDP – Instituto dos Vinhos do Douro e do Porto (ivdp.pt: introduction, special-categories, the-winemaking); Consejo Regulador D.O. Jerez-Xérès-Sherry (sherry.wine: types of sherry wine, ageing, what is fortification); apuntes del curso de sommelier, bloque E pp. 294–302

servicio.title: Service and Food Pairing
servicio.intro: By the end you'll know what temperature to serve each wine at, in which glass, how to open, store and decant it, how to spot a faulty wine and how to pair it with food.

chapters.lead: Temperature changes how you perceive a wine: too cold mutes the aromas, too warm emphasises the alcohol. Each style has its range.
points: Sparkling and sweet wines: well chilled, between 6 and 10 °C (sweet ones, 6–8 °C).
Light or medium-bodied whites and dry rosés: cold, between 7 and 10 °C.
Full-bodied and oaked whites: just cool, between 10 and 13 °C.
Light reds (Beaujolais type): slightly cool, around 13 °C.
Medium or full-bodied reds: 15–18 °C. Above 18 °C they lose freshness.
Fortified wines: tawny Port and oloroso Sherry, around 14–15 °C; fino and manzanilla, cold.

keys.t: The temperature at which a wine is best drunk so it shows its best.
A range of 6 to 10 °C, typical of sparkling and sweet wines.
In wine this means 15–18 °C, not the heat of a house in summer.
A bucket with water and ice to chill a bottle or keep it cold at the table.

quiz.q: At what temperature is a full-bodied red served?
quiz.ok: Between 15 and 18 °C
bad: At 25 °C, whatever the kitchen is like
quiz.why: Medium and full-bodied reds are served at cellar 'room temperature', 15–18 °C.

quiz.q: Which wines are served coldest?
quiz.ok: Sparkling and sweet wines
quiz.why: Sparkling and sweet wines are served well chilled, between 6 and 10 °C.

quiz.q: What happens if a red is served above 18 °C?
quiz.ok: It loses freshness and the alcohol stands out
bad: It becomes more acidic and lighter
quiz.why: Above about 18 °C the red loses freshness and the flavours turn heavy.

chapters.t: Glasses: shape and how much to pour
chapters.lead: The shape of the glass decides how aromas reach your nose. A good universal glass is all you need.
points: A wide bowl exposes more wine to the air and concentrates the aromas toward the rim.
The universal glass (a medium bowl that narrows a little at the top) works for reds, whites and sparkling wines.
For tasting, professionals use the standard tasting glass (ISO/AFNOR).
Hold it by the stem: you don't warm the wine and you don't smudge the bowl.
Don't fill it: about one third leaves room to swirl and smell. A 750 ml bottle gives 6 glasses of 125 ml.

keys.t: The part of the glass that holds the wine.
A glass of intermediate shape that works well with almost all wines.
A standardised glass tasters use to compare wines on equal terms.
The long foot of the glass, by which you hold it.

quiz.q: Why is it best to hold the glass by the stem?
quiz.ok: So your hand doesn't warm the wine
bad: So the wine makes more bubbles
quiz.why: A hand on the bowl warms the wine and also smudges the glass.

quiz.q: How full should a wine glass be?
quiz.ok: About a third
quiz.why: The free space lets you swirl the wine and gather the aromas.

quiz.q: How many 125 ml glasses come from a 750 ml bottle?
quiz.why: 750 divided by 125 gives 6 glasses.

chapters.lead: Opening a bottle well is a matter of calm. With sparkling wines, it is also a matter of safety.
points: Cut the foil below the lip, wipe the neck and pull the cork with a double-hinged corkscrew.
Sparkling wine: loosen the cage (6 half turns) but don't remove it; keep your hand over the cork at all times.
Tilt it to 45°, pointing away from people, and turn the bottle, not the cork. It should come out with a sigh, not a bang.
Pour in two stages: fill, let the foam settle and top up.
Several wines: from dry to sweet, from simple to complex and, generally, from young to old.

keys.t: A waiter's corkscrew with a two-step lever that removes the cork without breaking it.
The wire that holds the cork of a sparkling wine.
A sheet covering the neck and cork of the bottle.
The sequence in which several wines are served so none overshadows the next.

quiz.q: When opening a sparkling wine, what do you turn?
quiz.ok: The bottle, holding the cork firmly
bad: The cork, as fast as possible
Nothing: remove the cage and let it pop
quiz.why: Turning the bottle with your hand on the cork controls the pressure.

quiz.q: If you serve a dry white and a sweet wine, which goes first?
quiz.ok: The dry white
quiz.why: A sweet wine makes the dry one that follows taste sour.

quiz.q: At what angle do you hold a sparkling wine when opening it?
quiz.ok: About 45°
bad: Upright, with the neck pointing up
quiz.why: At 45° the pressure escapes in a controlled way and nothing spills.

chapters.lead: Wine is sensitive to heat, light and movement. And most wine is made to be drunk young, not kept for years.
points: A cool, stable place, ideally 10–15 °C. Worse than heat are sudden changes.
Bottles with natural cork go on their side: that way the cork doesn't dry out.
Darkness and stillness: light and vibration speed up ageing. The kitchen is a bad place.
Once open, stoppered and in the fridge: sparkling 1–3 days; light whites and rosés 5–7; reds 3–5; fortified wines about a month.
Few wines improve with age: those with high acidity, tannins or sugar, and fortified wines.

keys.t: The time a wine can spend in bottle improving or without losing quality.
The wearing down of wine through contact with air once it is open or badly sealed.
A wine's ability to improve over the years, which depends on its acidity, tannins, sugar and alcohol.
A stopper that removes air from the open bottle so it lasts a little longer.

quiz.q: Why are bottles with cork stored on their side?
quiz.ok: So the cork doesn't dry out
bad: So the wine takes on more colour
quiz.why: A moist cork keeps sealing well and lets no air in.

quiz.q: Which is a bad place to store wine?
quiz.ok: On top of the fridge, in the kitchen
quiz.why: The kitchen has heat and temperature swings, which harm wine.

quiz.q: Which wines tend to last the most years?
quiz.ok: Those with high acidity, tannins or sugar
quiz.why: Acidity, tannins, sugar and high alcohol protect the wine from oxidation.

chapters.lead: Decanting means pouring the wine into another container. It serves two purposes: separating the sediment and giving air to a young, closed wine.
points: Older reds and vintage Ports form sediment; whites almost never do.
Stand the bottle upright at least 24 hours beforehand so the sediment sinks.
Pour slowly and steadily, with a light under the neck; stop when the deposit appears.
Young, powerful reds, like many Tannats, can be decanted an hour or more beforehand to open up the aromas.
Very old wines are fragile: decant them just before serving, because they fade quickly.

keys.t: A glass jug into which wine is poured to separate it from the sediment or to aerate it.
A solid deposit of tannins, pigments and crystals formed by wines with age.
To expose a wine to air so it opens up its aromas.
A young wine that shows few aromas when opened.

quiz.q: Why is an old red decanted?
quiz.ok: To separate it from the sediment
quiz.why: With age, reds form a deposit and decanting leaves it behind in the bottle.

quiz.q: What should you do the day before decanting a wine with sediment?
quiz.ok: Stand the bottle upright
quiz.why: Upright, the sediment sinks to the bottom and is easier to separate.

quiz.q: Which wine is most delicate when decanting?
quiz.ok: A very old wine
quiz.why: Very old wines lose their aromas quickly once opened.

chapters.lead: Sometimes a wine is bad. Recognising the most common faults helps you tell whether it's the wine or your own taste.
points: Cork taint (TCA): smells of damp, wet cardboard or cellar, and the fruit fades. It isn't harmful, but it ruins the wine.
Oxidation: white turns amber or brown, red turns brick; it smells of cider or sherry and loses fruit.
Reduction: smell of rotten egg, burnt rubber or cabbage due to lack of oxygen; sometimes it improves with aeration.
Brett (Brettanomyces): a yeast that gives a smell of stable, sweaty leather or clove and smoke.
High volatile acidity: smells of vinegar or nail polish remover.

keys.t: Trichloroanisole, the compound responsible for the 'corked' or damp smell.
A fault caused by lack of oxygen that gives sulphurous smells, like rotten egg.
The yeast Brettanomyces, which gives animal or stable aromas.
Acetic acid and ethyl acetate; in excess, it smells of vinegar or nail polish remover.

quiz.q: A wine smells of wet cardboard and damp. What fault does it have?
quiz.ok: Cork taint (TCA)
quiz.why: TCA gives that typical smell of damp and wet cardboard.

quiz.q: What does a wine with high volatile acidity smell of?
quiz.ok: Vinegar or nail polish remover
quiz.why: Volatile acidity comes from acetic acid and ethyl acetate.

quiz.q: What can help a wine with reduction?
quiz.ok: Aerating or decanting it
quiz.why: Reduction comes from a lack of oxygen, and air can dissipate it.

chapters.t: Food pairing: how to match wine and food
chapters.lead: Pairing means making wine and food bring out the best in each other. There are few principles, but they almost always work.
points: Weight with weight: light dish with light wine, powerful dish with full-bodied wine.
The wine should be at least as acidic and as sweet as the dish, or more; otherwise it tastes flat or bitter.
Tannins are softened by protein and fat: that's why an asado (grilled beef) goes well with a tannic red like Tannat.
Salt softens tannins and suits fruity wines; alcohol amplifies chilli heat, and a touch of sweetness calms it.
Tannins and oily fish clash (metallic taste). And local often works: wines and dishes from the same region.

keys.t: Matching a wine with a dish so both shine.
How light or powerful a wine or dish feels in the mouth.
Compounds from grape skins and seeds that dry the mouth.
Matching a wine with the traditional food of its own region.

quiz.q: Why does a Tannat go well with an asado?
quiz.ok: Because protein and fat soften its tannins
bad: Because Tannat is a sweet wine
quiz.why: Protein and fat cushion the tannins and the wine feels rounder.

quiz.q: With a sweet dessert, which wine is best?
quiz.ok: One at least as sweet as the dessert
bad: A dry red with lots of tannin
quiz.why: If the dish is sweeter than the wine, the wine seems bitter.

quiz.q: With very spicy food, what should you avoid?
quiz.ok: A high-alcohol wine
bad: A wine with a touch of sweetness
quiz.why: Alcohol amplifies the sensation of heat.
